115

This page lists the 117 decisions that landed in the repository at a default while the batches ran, by theme, each with what was decided and why. A theme's Select button selects the theme for Speak, and an item's the item; a number in brackets leads to the item's sources at the bottom of its theme. The checker: typing and inference

141 142
143

Two type parameters solved together

144

A type parameter, such as T in f[\T\](x: T), is filled at each call by a static argument, written or inferred; the filled declaration is an instance. Walk fills a call's type parameters together. Read one at a time, the inference chapter would give the call below no answer; it is silent on the case, so no rule was chosen, and a test holds walk's answer.

145 
loneT[\S, T extends S\](a: T, b: T, s: S)
146	loneT(Apple, Pear, Pear)
147

Walk gives S and T both Fruit; one at a time, no T fits. [4]

148
149 150
151

No expected type inside try or atomic

152

The expected type is what the context asks for: x: RR64 = e asks RR64 of e. By your ruling, a typecase arm and a label body get it; a try block, its catch arms and an atomic block (one that runs as a single transaction) don't, and the inference chapter lists them as not yet described. The checker also takes the join, the least common supertype, of the finally block's type and the try's, which the text doesn't say. [5]

153
154 155
156

Ranking generics reached by conversion

157

When a call reaches several declarations only by conversion, and some are generic, the checker ranks them by their declared parameter types, else by the conversion order of their instances. The text is silent. The order keeps your rule that a conversion never changes which declaration runs: a plain declaration stays ahead of a generic one's narrow instance, and ZZ32 ahead of ZZ64. [52]

158
159 160
161

Which failed attempt the error names

162

The checker tries a call in up to four ways, such as plain and with conversion. When all fail, it reports the first way that had a candidate, so the message names a call that the rules could accept. One compiled test's message depends on it. [53]

163
164 165
166

spawn inside atomic, also in a function

167

spawn starts a parallel task; one inside an atomic block is a static error. The checker now finds it also inside a function expression within that block; before, such a program crashed the checker. The code generator has no spawn, so no compiled program changes. [55]

168
169 170
171

Conditional extends entries kept apart

172

A type may extend another under a condition, a where clause, which narrows where a declaration applies. Each such entry is now checked under its own condition, and the members under all. Below, Wrap needs an ordered E, which only the entry beside it assumes; the first version of the check accepted this, and the run failed at link time.

173 
object Bad[\E\](x: E) extends
174	  { Wrap[\E\], Shows where { E extends Ord[\E\] } }
175

Refused again, as before conditional extension was built. [175]

A header ignores the conditions

180

A declaration's header, meaning its type parameters and their bounds, its own where clause, throws, excludes and comprises, is checked under its own where clause only; its conditional extends entries, value parameters and members, under the conditions too. So a bound or an excludes entry that holds only under a condition is refused again. The value parameters' share is still open. [176]

The same conversion on every candidate

199

Below, a call with a ZZ32 needs the same conversion, to ZZ64, on all three declarations. The checker refuses it as ambiguous, rather than typing it by what the three return types share. It accepts the three declarations, though the text says such a set is not valid.

Coverage judged in each providing type

209

A functional method has self among its parameters and is called as f(x); a closed trait's comprises clause lists every type below it. Whether two functional methods over closed traits cover their overlap is judged in each type that provides both, so a trait between them that adds nothing of its own is refused by the compiler and runs under walk. The compiler's verdict can also depend on what it compiled earlier, so no test holds it. [8]

214

When a name has a generic and a plain declaration, a call that writes its static argument runs different code on the two paths. The text is silent, so no rule was chosen; a test holds walk's answer.

216	opw(a: ZZ64, b: ZZ64)
217	opw[\ZZ64\](z, w)    (* z: ZZ32, w: ZZ64 *)

Walk runs the generic; compiled code, the plain one. [10]

Functions and functional methods don't mix

223

Both paths refuse a set of overloads over two closed traits that mixes a top-level function with functional methods: the rules for both kinds apply, and neither says which governs. So String's four sets of concatenation operators are top-level only; the check of operators found no other such set in the library. [11]

The comprises check matches by names

228

The compiler's comprises check, 14 lines that you approved, matches types by how they spell their type variable and by simple names, so an unrelated trait of the same name counts, and a false clause can pass. A test of the failure records the defect; nothing on microGPT's path waits on a repair. [13]

The return-type rule at every instance

233

Where one overload is more specific than another, its return type must fit the other's. The checker checks this at every instance of a generic declaration, so it also refuses a generic declaration beside a plain one over an object type, which Park's 2019 paper would let through. You chose this construction for overloads that differ in their type parameters; no library declaration is refused. [57]

235 236

Methods in closed traits count for coverage

238

When the checker asks whether a set of overloads covers every case of a closed trait, it reads the self of a functional method declared inside each listed trait as that trait, so those methods count. [59]

self compared as a receiver

243

The Meet Rule asks that two overlapping overloads have a third declared at their overlap. Where a type inherits an operator's overloads from several traits, the checker now treats self, wherever it sits, as it treats the x of a dotted call x.f(). This cleared six refused IN declarations in the library. [63]

Object expressions and their closed traits

248

An object expression, object extends T ... end, makes a value of an unnamed type. When T sits below a closed trait, the checker now checks it against the comprises clause of every closed trait above it, as the traits chapter reads. [65]

A widening override at every instance

253

An override that widens an inherited method's parameter, say from ZZ32 to Number, must return a type that fits the inherited return at every instance; before, every widening override was refused. An object below a trait that redeclares an inherited method abstract must now define it. No library declaration is refused. [66]

Generic pairs that exclude only together

258

Two generic declarations whose parameter types exclude each other only taken together are a valid pair on both paths: below, b fixes one T for both parameters, so no argument fits both. You chose this on 17 October without a reason. The reason now on record, the type group's 2011 paper, replaced one that a review found was the revival's own text; the rule stands either way.

260	o[\T\](x: Q[\T\], b: Box[\T\])

Valid on both paths. [228]

Your decision on closed traits now states as a requirement, not a reason, that the checker uses their coverage only to accept a set of overloads and to settle a tie between most specific declarations, never to decide subtyping: the soundness proof covers only that use, and not a call that needs a conversion. It was applied at your word of 22 October, without your review of each change. [276]

A type inherits a declaration unless one of its own override declarations overrides it; an override elsewhere in the hierarchy doesn't hide it. Walk and the checker read it so, each held by a test. [69]

A typecase picks an arm by a value's run-time type. An arm that names a type nobody declared is now refused when walk loads the program; before, it failed only when that arm ran.

A reduction combines the values of a big operator such as SUM, and its simpleJoin combines two of them. A program's own reduction must give simpleJoin at its own element type; the team's old spelling at Any ran before and is refused at load now. No test or demo declares one, and a test holds the refusal. [72]

override at the same types refused

An override must widen the inherited parameter types, as the chapter's “strict subtype” says; one at the same types overrides nothing, and walk refuses the program at load with “does not override any inherited declaration”. A redeclaration without override replaces a method at the same types. The checker doesn't check the modifier yet. [73]

321

Walk checks an override once, at the generic declaration's own type parameters, not again at each instance. So an override whose types happen to equal the inherited ones at one instance is accepted. [74]

An override f[\T extends Number\](x: T) over an inherited f(x: ZZ32) is a static error, though some of its instances would override. No program in the tree writes it. [75]

A comprehension builds a collection from a generator, a source of values, as below; 0#3 is the integers 0 to 2. A program can't add a type below Number

408

The library closes Number with a comprises clause, so a program may not add a number type below it; the specification gives Number no such clause. The team's test “We ought to be able to extend the builtin type Number” runs only because walk doesn't check the library's clauses at load. [23]

A comparison with NaN answers false

413

On both paths <, <=, > and >= with a NaN answer false, as RR64's own < does and as the rationals chapter says, “for compatibility with floating-point arithmetic”; the tuple comparisons follow. ℚ holds the infinities

418

Fortress revival · 5 November 2026

What was decided

This page lists the 117 decisions that landed in the repository at a default while the batches ran, by theme, each with what was decided and why. A theme's Select button selects the theme for Speak, and an item's the item; a number in brackets leads to the item's sources at the bottom of its theme. Nothing here waits on you: each stands as it landed, and one word from you still changes any of them.

Themes

  • The checker: typing and inference (7)
  • Overloading: shared names, and which declaration runs (12)
  • Walk's checks when it loads a program (8)
  • Walk's choice of declaration and instance (7)
  • Numbers and numerals (14)
  • Sizes and arrays (5)
  • Ranges (5)
  • The library: generators, strings, comparisons and reductions (21)
  • The library's native bindings (3)
  • The specification's text (18)
  • Components and their apis (4)
  • Tests and the team's demos (2)
  • Code generation and the run time (5)
  • What each batch changed (6)
  • Words used on this page

The checker: typing and inference

Two type parameters solved together

A type parameter, such as T in f[\T\](x: T), is filled at each call by a static argument, written or inferred; the filled declaration is an instance. Walk fills a call's type parameters together. Read one at a time, the inference chapter would give the call below no answer; it is silent on the case, so no rule was chosen, and a test holds walk's answer.

loneT[\S, T extends S\](a: T, b: T, s: S)
loneT(Apple, Pear, Pear)

Walk gives S and T both Fruit; one at a time, no T fits. [4]

No expected type inside try or atomic

The expected type is what the context asks for: x: RR64 = e asks RR64 of e. By your ruling, a typecase arm and a label body get it; a try block, its catch arms and an atomic block (one that runs as a single transaction) don't, and the inference chapter lists them as not yet described. The checker also takes the join, the least common supertype, of the finally block's type and the try's, which the text doesn't say. [5]

Ranking generics reached by conversion

When a call reaches several declarations only by conversion, and some are generic, the checker ranks them by their declared parameter types, else by the conversion order of their instances. The text is silent. The order keeps your rule that a conversion never changes which declaration runs: a plain declaration stays ahead of a generic one's narrow instance, and ZZ32 ahead of ZZ64. [52]

Which failed attempt the error names

The checker tries a call in up to four ways, such as plain and with conversion. When all fail, it reports the first way that had a candidate, so the message names a call that the rules could accept. One compiled test's message depends on it. [53]

spawn inside atomic, also in a function

spawn starts a parallel task; one inside an atomic block is a static error. The checker now finds it also inside a function expression within that block; before, such a program crashed the checker. The code generator has no spawn, so no compiled program changes. [55]

Conditional extends entries kept apart

A type may extend another under a condition, a where clause, which narrows where a declaration applies. Each such entry is now checked under its own condition, and the members under all. Below, Wrap needs an ordered E, which only the entry beside it assumes; the first version of the check accepted this, and the run failed at link time.

object Bad[\E\](x: E) extends
  { Wrap[\E\], Shows where { E extends Ord[\E\] } }

Refused again, as before conditional extension was built. [175]

A header ignores the conditions

A declaration's header, meaning its type parameters and their bounds, its own where clause, throws, excludes and comprises, is checked under its own where clause only; its conditional extends entries, value parameters and members, under the conditions too. So a bound or an excludes entry that holds only under a condition is refused again. The value parameters' share is still open. [176]

References
  • [4] row 613; F-141; InferLoneBoundMentionsParamWalk.fss.
  • [5] REPORT.md, section 10.
  • [52] P-46.
  • [175] P-151; trait-parameters.tex; XXXCondExtendUnconditionalEntryChecker.fss.
  • [176] 5b11849c6; row 781; TypeWellFormedChecker.scala.

Overloading: shared names, and which declaration runs

The same conversion on every candidate

Below, a call with a ZZ32 needs the same conversion, to ZZ64, on all three declarations. The checker refuses it as ambiguous, rather than typing it by what the three return types share. It accepts the three declarations, though the text says such a set is not valid.

choose(a: S, b: ZZ64)
choose(a: T, b: ZZ64)
choose(a: V, b: ZZ64)
choose(x, n)    (* x fits all three; n: ZZ32 *)

Refused: “Ambiguous coercion”. [7]

Coverage judged in each providing type

A functional method has self among its parameters and is called as f(x); a closed trait's comprises clause lists every type below it. Whether two functional methods over closed traits cover their overlap is judged in each type that provides both, so a trait between them that adds nothing of its own is refused by the compiler and runs under walk. The compiler's verdict can also depend on what it compiled earlier, so no test holds it. [8]

A written static argument on a mixed name

When a name has a generic and a plain declaration, a call that writes its static argument runs different code on the two paths. The text is silent, so no rule was chosen; a test holds walk's answer.

opw[\T extends Number\](a: T, b: T)
opw(a: ZZ64, b: ZZ64)
opw[\ZZ64\](z, w)    (* z: ZZ32, w: ZZ64 *)

Walk runs the generic; compiled code, the plain one. [10]

Functions and functional methods don't mix

Both paths refuse a set of overloads over two closed traits that mixes a top-level function with functional methods: the rules for both kinds apply, and neither says which governs. So String's four sets of concatenation operators are top-level only; the check of operators found no other such set in the library. [11]

The comprises check matches by names

The compiler's comprises check, 14 lines that you approved, matches types by how they spell their type variable and by simple names, so an unrelated trait of the same name counts, and a false clause can pass. A test of the failure records the defect; nothing on microGPT's path waits on a repair. [13]

The return-type rule at every instance

Where one overload is more specific than another, its return type must fit the other's. The checker checks this at every instance of a generic declaration, so it also refuses a generic declaration beside a plain one over an object type, which Park's 2019 paper would let through. You chose this construction for overloads that differ in their type parameters; no library declaration is refused. [57]

Methods in closed traits count for coverage

When the checker asks whether a set of overloads covers every case of a closed trait, it reads the self of a functional method declared inside each listed trait as that trait, so those methods count. [59]

self compared as a receiver

The Meet Rule asks that two overlapping overloads have a third declared at their overlap. Where a type inherits an operator's overloads from several traits, the checker now treats self, wherever it sits, as it treats the x of a dotted call x.f(). This cleared six refused IN declarations in the library. [63]

Object expressions and their closed traits

An object expression, object extends T ... end, makes a value of an unnamed type. When T sits below a closed trait, the checker now checks it against the comprises clause of every closed trait above it, as the traits chapter reads. [65]

A widening override at every instance

An override that widens an inherited method's parameter, say from ZZ32 to Number, must return a type that fits the inherited return at every instance; before, every widening override was refused. An object below a trait that redeclares an inherited method abstract must now define it. No library declaration is refused. [66]

Generic pairs that exclude only together

Two generic declarations whose parameter types exclude each other only taken together are a valid pair on both paths: below, b fixes one T for both parameters, so no argument fits both. You chose this on 17 October without a reason. The reason now on record, the type group's 2011 paper, replaced one that a review found was the revival's own text; the rule stands either way.

o[\T\](x: P[\T\], b: Box[\T\])
o[\T\](x: Q[\T\], b: Box[\T\])

Valid on both paths. [228]

Coverage serves the overloading rules only

Your decision on closed traits now states as a requirement, not a reason, that the checker uses their coverage only to accept a set of overloads and to settle a tie between most specific declarations, never to decide subtyping: the soundness proof covers only that use, and not a call that needs a conversion. It was applied at your word of 22 October, without your review of each change. [276]

References
  • [7] row 391; overloading.tex.
  • [8] row 547.
  • [10] row 504; DispatchWrittenStaticArgWalk.fss.
  • [11] row 545; F-281; REPORT.md, section 12.
  • [13] rows 489, 490.
  • [57] P-45; F-75; row 542.
  • [65] row 597.
  • [228] P-152; 14e91723f; exc-reduction.tick.
  • [276] P-60; F-76; rows 543, 551; 4d7df29c3.

Walk's checks when it loads a program

comprises at load: main component only

Walk checks the comprises clauses of the main component only, at load; the checker reads every clause. Checking all of them under walk would refuse every program that imports Reflect, four of the team's tests and two demos that extend Number or Exception. [15]

Inheritance and a type's own override

A type inherits a declaration unless one of its own override declarations overrides it; an override elsewhere in the hierarchy doesn't hide it. Walk and the checker read it so, each held by a test. [69]

self compared at the same position

When the traits chapter compares two declarations' parameter types, walk now compares the self parameter at the same position, as the checker does. [70]

An undeclared type in a typecase arm

A typecase picks an arm by a value's run-time type. An arm that names a type nobody declared is now refused when walk loads the program; before, it failed only when that arm ran.

typecase x of Foo => 1 else => 0 end    (* no Foo *)

Refused at load. [71]

A reduction's simpleJoin at Any

A reduction combines the values of a big operator such as SUM, and its simpleJoin combines two of them. A program's own reduction must give simpleJoin at its own element type; the team's old spelling at Any ran before and is refused at load now. No test or demo declares one, and a test holds the refusal. [72]

override at the same types refused

An override must widen the inherited parameter types, as the chapter's “strict subtype” says; one at the same types overrides nothing, and walk refuses the program at load with “does not override any inherited declaration”. A redeclaration without override replaces a method at the same types. The checker doesn't check the modifier yet. [73]

An override checked once

Walk checks an override once, at the generic declaration's own type parameters, not again at each instance. So an override whose types happen to equal the inherited ones at one instance is accepted. [74]

An override over a narrower inherited type

An override f[\T extends Number\](x: T) over an inherited f(x: ZZ32) is a static error, though some of its instances would override. No program in the tree writes it. [75]

References
  • [15] rows 551, 595, 596, 597.
  • [69] row 615.
  • [72] ReductionSimpleJoinAtAnyWalk.fss.
  • [73] OverrideEqualTypesWalk.fss; row 653.
  • [74] F-147.

Walk's choice of declaration and instance

The plain declaration runs, not the generic

An Apple and a Cherry share two closest supertypes, Red and Round. For the call below, walk runs the plain declaration, as before, without weighing the generic one at its bound; a test records the gap. Without the bound, the pair is now refused at load, as two declarations of the same types.

g(a: Any, b: Any)
g[\T extends Fruit\](a: T, b: T)
g(Apple, Cherry)

Walk runs g(a: Any, b: Any). [18]

The open type is chosen first

Under walk, a type parameter whose bound names itself, as T extends Ord[\T\], stays open when nothing fixes it, and every value passes it. In a Holder[\OPEN\], take(x: T) then runs for 3, not take(x: ZZ32), and accepts a string; for tuples, below, it goes the other way. A written static argument avoids both.

pick(x: Any)
pick(x: (T, T))
pick((1, 2))    (* in a Holder[\OPEN\] *)

Walk runs pick(x: Any). [19]

The open type prints as OPEN

Where walk can't fix a type parameter, it leaves it open and prints it as OPEN, as in BoxU[\OPEN\]. The word can be renamed at any time. [83]

A where bound stays on its own trait

A where clause that bounds one trait's type parameter no longer bounds another declaration's parameter, as the overloading chapter says.

trait W[\T\] where { T extends ZZ32 } end
p[\U\](x: U): String = "U"
p(x: ZZ32): String = "ZZ32"

p(3) is "ZZ32"; walk ran the generic before. [84]

Walk instantiates at the value's type

Walk has no static types, so where a variable is declared wider than its value, as x: Number = 3, walk runs a generic call at the value's type, ZZ32, and the compiled path at Number. The same generic body runs at two instances, and the values agree. [85]

A program's own coerce in a generic call

When a generic call's arguments have different types, both paths may now convert them to a common instance by the program's own coerce, not only by the library's. [87]

An unwritten static argument of a reduction

A comprehension builds a collection from a generator, a source of values, as below; 0#3 is the integers 0 to 2. When one, or a reduction, leaves its static argument unwritten, walk now takes its value's declared type, else the join of its elements' run-time types, else the bound; it gave the empty type before. So emptyRSum(0), declared RR64, is 0.0, not 0. New to you: a declared type that doesn't fit is dropped with no warning, so u: Number = SUM[j <- 0#3] j is the integer 3.

xs: List[\ZZ32\] = <| 2 k | k <- 0#3 |>

<|0, 2, 4|>; walk refused it before. [210]

References
  • [18] row 589; F-141.
  • [19] row 663; OpenTupleDispatchWalk.fss.
  • [84] row 692; WhereBoundOverloadWalk.fss.
  • [85] P-46; F-137; row 509.
  • [210] F-228; 20474c144.

Numbers and numerals

A program can't add a type below Number

The library closes Number with a comprises clause, so a program may not add a number type below it; the specification gives Number no such clause. The team's test “We ought to be able to extend the builtin type Number” runs only because walk doesn't check the library's clauses at load. [23]

A comparison with NaN answers false

On both paths <, <=, > and >= with a NaN answer false, as RR64's own < does and as the rationals chapter says, “for compatibility with floating-point arithmetic”; the tuple comparisons follow. The overview of operators says such a comparison raises FloatingComparisonError, which both libraries declare and nothing raises. [24]

ℚ holds the infinities

The revised number chapter reads ℚ, the type QQ, as holding +∞, −∞ and 0/0, so some laws of arithmetic fail in it and not every two values compare. QQ no longer inherits check and check_star from RR64. Your ruling that QQ's ceiling and truncate raise at the infinities stands. [25]

A numeral is read as its nearest double

A numeral with a decimal point is read as its nearest double, not as the exact rational it denotes. A test records the gap; no other way was chosen.

round(2.50000000000000001)

2 on both paths; the exact value rounds to 3. [28]

ZZ32 with NN32 runs at ZZ64

Neither ZZ32 nor NN32 holds every value of the other, so an operation on one of each runs at ZZ64, the narrowest type that holds both. The compiler's prelude gives ZZ until the switch-over removes it.

a: ZZ32 = -1
b: NN32 = 3
a + b

2, a ZZ64. [89]

Float numerals stay as they were

On the compiled path, an integer numeral such as 3 now has its own type, which converts to the integer or float type a call needs; under walk it is still a ZZ32. A numeral with a decimal point, such as 0.5, is unchanged. [92]

Each integer type declares its own unsigned

The Integral trait, which the integer types share, no longer declares unsigned in its api, since its one return type would refuse a valid program. Each integer type declares its own, as ZZ64 does. [94]

A numeral too large for every overload

If no overload of a call takes a numeral's value, the checker refuses the call, rather than choosing the narrowest declaration that would hold it.

f(x: ZZ32)
f(x: NN32)
f(5000000000)

Refused: the value fits neither type. [96]

A numeral fits only a type that holds it

A numeral becomes a value of a type only if that type holds it. The specification makes the error below static; the compiled path raises it at run time today, and the defect is recorded.

x: NN32 = -1

An error: NN32 holds no negative number. [97]

A huge ZZ power raises IntegerOverflow

ZZ has no fixed width, yet under walk a ZZ or numeral power whose exponent is above 2^31 − 1, or whose result Java's BigInteger can't hold, raises IntegerOverflow for every base but 0, 1 and −1, as the operators chapter's overflow rule reads. [196]

An integer power answers an integer

Each integer type's ^ answers its own type, the numeral's too, so a negative exponent raises, rather than giving a fraction. A fraction comes from a float or rational base.

2^(-1)

Raises IntegerOverflow, where walk gave 0.5. [201]

Nonzero float over zero gives infinity

On both paths a nonzero float divided by zero gives an infinity, as IEEE 754 says and the team's constant below relies on; the specification's sentence says it “produces a NaN value”. The conflict is recorded; if IEEE 754 governs, a later revision fixes the sentence.

infinity : RR64 = 1.0 / 0.0

+∞ on both paths. [336]

nextUp and nextDown at a signed zero

On RR64 and RR32, nextUp(-0.0) is 0.0 and nextDown(0.0) is -0.0: the team's directed rounding steps in IEEE's total order, where −0 sits just below +0. IEEE 754-2008, and Java's Math.nextUp, give the smallest subnormal. A test asserts today's values; no directed rounding reaches the case. [344]

ZZ's CHOOSE out of range answers 1

ZZ's CHOOSE, the binomial coefficient, answers 1 where the specification's zero rule and the four fixed-width types answer 0: at k < 0, or k > n for a natural n. The value was kept when its Java code moved to a helper, with a test that records the gap; one guard would give 0.

big(3) CHOOSE big(5)

1; the specification says 0. [348]

References

  • [24] row 672.

Sizes and arrays

Two size parameters counted as different

A nat parameter is a size that the type carries. In two[\nat a, nat b\] the checker counts a and b as different, so a typecase arm that needs them equal is refused as unreachable, though the team's own questions and answers say a parameter may equal any size it is instantiated at. A test records it; nothing on the path builds on it. [32]

Size arithmetic past ZZ64 stops

Under walk, a size written as arithmetic in a type, such as n + m, is computed in ZZ64; a step that leaves ZZ64 stops the program with an error rather than wrapping silently. No program writes such sizes. [98]

Vector operations build through replica

The library's vector and matrix operations +, -, unary -, scale and pmul now build their result through the argument's replica, a fresh array of the same shape, and cast it back. A user type below Vector whose replica answers a plain array gets CastError there, where it once got that array. [198]

Row and column subscripts in the api

The api now declares a matrix's whole-row and whole-column subscripts, so a checker that reads the api sees them, not only walk.

m[:, j]    m[i, :]

Column j and row i of m. [199]

No immutable arrays of rank 2 or 3

The library has no immutable arrays of rank 2 or 3 (two or three dimensions), so the api's factories for them, which no program could call, are now a comment, and leave the library chapter that renders the api. [202]

  • [202] FortressLibrary.fsi.

Ranges

An empty range prints as the library's one

A range of length zero, written MIN # 0 or the like, is now the library's one empty range, so it prints bounds other than the ones written. [102]

Range runs that stopped now give values

Under walk, flip, the subscripts of rank 2 and 3 with bounds and indices, a strided seq, shifts and UniformDistribution used to stop with an error, and now give values. [103]

A reversed mapped range prints differently

Mapping a function over a whole range now gives a new library object. Its elements and order are unchanged, but its reverse prints differently.

seq(0:6:2).map(fn x => x + 1).reverse

Prints SimpleReversedIndexed(mapped(seq(1,3,5,7))), not mapped(7,5,3,1). [104]

Two whole open ranges compare as equal

Comparing two whole open ranges, (:) CMP (:), now answers EqualTo; walk stopped there before. [105]

truncL and truncR return a bounded range

truncL and truncR, which cut a range at one end, are declared to return a range bounded at both ends. The team's narrower types, a range with a left or a right end, are true, but no body could show them to the checker. [106]

The library: generators, strings, comparisons and reductions

The fused big operator's result type

A big operator, such as SUM or BIG MAX, reduces a generator's values to one. The library's fused path, which combines one reduction with an outer one, as in a maximum of sums, answered its input type where it declares its output type; its result now passes through cast[\O0\], the library's way to type a branch that a typecase can't. When the operators fuse is unchanged. [40]

Comparisons get MIN and MAX

You asked for this explanation. TotalComparison is the type of LessThan, EqualTo and GreaterThan. BIG MIN and BIG MAX are declared only for types that extend StandardMinMax, the library's mark for “has MIN and MAX”, so without that parent the reduction below found no declaration under walk. The parent, which the library's other ordered types have, changes no other answer.

BIG MIN [c <- cs] c    (* cs: comparisons *)

Runs; walk found no declaration before. [109]

ANDCOND of two relational predicates

A repair of the library's conditions changed this under walk: two relational predicates, a kind of filter condition, combined in a program by ANDCOND give a plain predicate, no longer a relational one. Its value is unchanged.

relational[\ZZ32\](p1 ANDCOND p2)

false; it was true. [111]

fill and tabulate declared once

fill and tabulate are declared once, where the array traits meet, so a type that inherits several array traits gets one declaration. Vector and Matrix also declare them at their own type, so v.fill(0.0) on a vector gives a vector. [112]

Names of the tabulating factories

The factories that build an array from a function of its index are named tabulatedArray1, tabulatedArray2, tabulatedArray3 and tabulatedVector. [113]

Slip repairs changed walk's output

Repairs of small slips in the library changed what walk prints for mapped generators, BIG MINMAX, split, avFlat and UniformDistribution. [114]

String repairs, and a strided slice

Repairs of the string library changed five values that walk prints. A slice with an implicit start and a stride counts from the string's right end, where the specification's reading starts at the left; a test records the gap.

"abcdef"[:3:2]

bd; the specification's reading gives ac. [116]

Case-insensitive comparison by the contract

CASE_INSENSITIVE_CMP on strings is now defined by the library's own ensures clause, the stated property of its result, not by a case folding of characters that no library string uses. [117]

The string api exports three internal types

The string api now exports three of the team's internal types, Concatenable, Balanceable and SubString's constructor, so the components that build strings can name them. [120]

Test helpers changed under walk

Under walk, shouldRaise with nothing raised now throws a ForbiddenException that its own catch doesn't take; assert on tuples prints a FAIL line; and partition at ZZ64 is refused. [121]

Six declarations' printed values

Six library declarations now print what their bodies state, and an ill-typed reduction that answered 3 is now refused. [122]

A transposed matrix's uncalled methods

A transposed matrix keeps its add, subtract and negate methods, which now pass the checker though nothing calls them; its + runs Matrix's operator. [125]

An immutable sub-array lost its put

An immutable sub-array had a put, which nothing called and which contradicts immutability. It is removed, so such a call now fails at the call. [126]

New declarations modelled on the team's

The library gained 16 range declarations in its api, a lazy LEXICO on Comparison, which combines comparisons in dictionary order, and SimpleIndexValuePairs, each modelled on a declaration that the team wrote. [127]

members keeps declaration order

Reflect's members of an object now lists them in the order declared, not as a sorted set. [128]

Sliced index-value pairs keep indices

Slicing the index-value pairs of a list keeps each pair's original index, as before, rather than renumbering from 0 as a set's pairs do. [129]

Index-value pairs above index 0

For a value whose indices start above 0, its default index-value pairs now carry those indices, as the arrays' range subscript and the ranges chapter do; an array's own pairs stay numbered by position. Two answers changed. [130]

Predicates read in the sequence's order

A relational predicate such as increasing now reads a sequence in its own order, where it read positions 0 to n − 1 before.

increasing((0#4).reverse)

Now false. [132]

isLeftZero of Unordered is refused

isLeftZero tells whether a comparison decides a lexicographic result alone. Your answer declared its true case over total comparisons: LessThan and GreaterThan answer true, EqualTo false. Unordered, a comparison that isn't total, matches no declaration, so walk refuses isLeftZero(Unordered); nothing in the library calls it. [211]

Tuple comparisons need ordered elements

The library's ten tuple comparison operators now require each element to be partially ordered, where they compared elements of any type. Your “Agreed.” of 20 October took this without the three costs below. A pair of floats stays ordered, and a where clause, now buildable, could lift the refusals at any time.

(1, ()) < (2, ())
(1, 2) < (1, 2.5)
((1, 2), 3) < ((1, 3), 0)

All refused; the first was true, and only walk refuses the second. [213]

When to write a reduction's static argument

Your rule: write a reduction's static argument where nothing at the call fixes its element type. Today the checker fixes it from none of the generators, the body or a declared type, and refuses every such SUM or PROD, so the library and both microGPT programs write it in every form.

matOffset(i: ZZ32): ZZ32 = SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#i] matCount(j)

Compiles; without [\ZZ32\] the checker refuses it. [269]

A where variable in an extends clause

The revised specification says “a where-clause variable may not appear as a static argument in an extends clause”. Its reason covers only a variable that may stand for more than one type; below, each S extends at most one Baz, so gives one Bar: the reason allows it, and the sentence refuses it. Both paths refuse every such declaration, so the text still describes what runs. You asked for this plain explanation.

trait Foo[\S\] extends Bar[\T\]
  where { S extends Baz[\T\] }

Refused on both paths. [41]

The dotted Meet Rule keeps its exact form

Two overlapping dotted methods of one type are valid together only if a third is declared at exactly the intersection of their parameter types, as the 2011 Working Draft wrote it. The rules for functions and functional methods were revised to Park's paper; no decision covered the dotted form, so it stays, and Appendix I names it as open. [133]

makeSet keeps its old explanation

The overloading chapter still explains its makeSet pair as ambiguous at makeSet(3, 4). Under the chapter's present rules, one declaration is more specific, and the return-type rule, checked at every instance, refuses the pair where it is declared. No decision asked for a new explanation, so the team's stays. [134]

Three more passages revised

Three more passages now agree with the overloading decisions: when a dotted call applies, the assumption about a call's static variables, and the promise that the compiler can always find the most specific declaration statically. That promise now has an exception: with type parameters, the most specific declaration may be known only at run time. [135]

Five sentences on Park's paper

Five sentences link the revised overloading text to Park's 2019 paper: a citation of its rule for one trait; the position-by-position comparison of two generic declarations, as a limit of the compiled path, not a language rule; a note that its soundness proof doesn't cover the library's SUM, BIG MAX and Integral families; a sentence on its main theorem; and its default bound Any. [136]

A block's earlier elements left off

In do f(x); g(y) end, every element but the last must have type (), and the checker has always checked that. The inference chapter's list of the places where an expected type guides inference leaves this one out; the list was kept as measured on the checker. [137]

Varargs keep the text's HeapSequence

The specification gives a varargs parameter xs: T... the type HeapSequence[\T\], which no library declares; both paths give it ImmutableArray[\T, ZZ32\]. The sentence stands, with a revision box that says what both do. [138]

comprises read at the level of values

A comprises clause is read at the level of values: each listed type extends the closed trait, maybe through another trait, and a generic subtrait with the closed trait's own type parameters is allowed. The text, like both checkers, reads “every type that extends it” as the direct extenders, so it refuses a two-level subtrait whose every value is listed, though walk runs it. [139]

Two notations: factorial and midpoint

The integer chapter defines the factorial by 0! = 1 and (m+1)! = (m+1) m!, in place of the Working Draft's product, and writes a midpoint as lo + (hi − lo) DIV 2, in place of the team's floorAverage, which the one library doesn't declare. [140]

BlockedRange respelled over ZZ32

Since ranges became ZZ32 ranges, the chapter on defining generators spells its adapted BlockedRange example over ZZ32, as its two earlier passages were, so that it runs on today's library. [141]

ℚ's listing gained four algebraic traits

The specification's ℚ now extends the traits that the library declares on QQ: StandardPartialOrder, StandardMinMax, AdditiveGroup and MultiplicativeRing. A new sentence says their laws, such as x − x = 0, hold for finite rationals and need not hold where 0/0 or an infinity takes part, as on RR64 they need not hold with a NaN. [142]

narrow stated on ZZ

The integer chapter now states narrow on ZZ, the conversion that takes an unbounded integer to a fixed width by truncation, as the library declares it; a test's comment was reworded to match. [143]

An oversized GCD or LCM raises

A GCD or LCM whose result doesn't fit its fixed-width type raises IntegerOverflow, as all fixed-width integer arithmetic does. Walk does so on NN32 and NN64 today; the compiled path follows at the switch-over. [145]

What the inference chapter covers

The new inference chapter covers type parameters and the size kinds nat and int, and names bool, dim, unit and operator parameters as not described, rather than stating a general rule with refusals in a box. [146]

How a call's static arguments are found

The inference chapter now states this. The declaration is chosen first, by conversion resolution. A lone type parameter takes the narrowest of its arguments' types and the types they convert to; where none is narrowest, as for a ZZ64 and an RR64, it takes their union, and nothing converts. The expected type guides inference only in the listed contexts; a box states walk's inference from run-time types. [147]

extends Any means Object

A trait or object declared extends Any is made an Object, by the traits chapter's rule. The specification's own trait Tuple extends Any excludes { Object }, and roots such as BinaryPredicate, don't fit the rule, but no library declares them yet; the default is to name Tuple beside Any and Object when one does. [190]

Unit factors at a negative power

Since an integer to a negative power raises IntegerOverflow, the dimensions chapter's factors, such as 2.54 × 10^(-2) for the inch and 10^(-1) to 10^(-24) for the prefixes, would raise if run. Units aren't built, so nothing runs them, and the chapter stays as the team wrote it until they are. [200]

The CHOOSE identity fails at −1

The specification's identity below is false at m = n = −1 under its own zero rule: (-1) CHOOSE (-1) and (-1) CHOOSE 0 are 0, but 0 CHOOSE 0 is 1. Both paths follow the zero rule, no program states the identity, and no way was chosen, so the text stands.

(m CHOOSE n) + (m CHOOSE (n+1)) = ((m+1) CHOOSE (n+1))

At m = n = −1: 0 + 0 = 1, false. [333]

Components and their apis

A component returns exactly its api's type

A component is a unit of Fortress code, and its api the interface it exports. A component's function or method must declare exactly its api's return type: a narrower one, which the text allows, is refused, since a compiled call names the api's header and would fail with NoSuchMethodError. Appendix I names the departure.

f(): Number          (* in the api *)
f(): ZZ32 = 3        (* in the component *)

Refused. [291]

Type parameters named as in the api

A component must name an exported generic declaration's type parameters as its api does: compiled code names a generic template by its parameters, so a client's call would fail to load it. The text names no rule; the library uses one name on both sides. [292]

No var on an object's parameter in an api

An api may not write var on an object's value parameter: the team's parser refuses it, though the api grammar admits it, and the prose says abstract field declarations take no var. A component may still write it, as in OneShot(var canTryIt: Boolean); whether the export rule allows that is open. [293]

A field satisfies an api's abstract getter

A component trait's field x: ZZ32 satisfies the api's abstract getter x(): ZZ32, so such a program, which ran before the export check was completed, still does. The other way, an api's field met by a component's getter, which the text allows, is still refused. [294]

Tests and the team's demos

Three lines of the team's tests rewritten

A type parameter written without a bound is bounded by Any, which holds () and tuples. So the team's doubledOverloading.fss would be refused as written: a() passes (), which also fits its sibling. It now writes extends Object; every assertion is kept, and two pinned messages lost their printed extends Object.

a() = 0
a[\E\](v: E) = 1

Refused as written; now a[\E extends Object\](v: E). [304]

The APL program's first compile error moved

The APL microGPT program's first compile error moved, at the same phase, from “DelegatedIndexed is undefined.” to “ImmutableArray is undefined.”: the List api now imports a type that names ImmutableArray, which the compiler's prelude lacks. The flat program doesn't import List; the error goes when the compiled path reads the one library. [305]

References
  • [304] 1bc0a9083; F-296; doubledOverloading.fss.

Code generation and the run time

The code generator refuses override

The code generator refuses a method declared override, so the team's disp0.fss, which the checker now accepts, doesn't compile. What compiled dispatch does with a declaration a type no longer provides is open; neither the library nor microGPT declares an override. [44]

The compiler's prelude isn't repaired

The compiler's prelude isn't repaired: its known defects, such as its swapped spellings of the wrapping and saturating operators and its ZZ64 shift, stay, each held by a test, until the switch-over deletes it. Since 3 November the rule covers the prelude's own text only: a shared Java helper, once fixed for the one library, changes the prelude's value too. [217]

The compiled drandom depends on scheduling

The compiled drandom, whose name promises the same values each run, gives values that depend on the task schedule above one thread: a tree of tasks that drew at every node summed to three values in three runs at four threads. It's no data race; only the compiler's prelude binds it, so it goes at the switch-over, and microGPT draws no random numbers. [334]

Own where variables fail at run time

A function or method whose own where clause introduces a new type variable now compiles and links, where the code generator used to refuse it, and its compiled call fails at run time with NoClassDefFoundError: the failure still shows, but at run time, not at compile time. No library declaration has the form; one condition would restore the refusal. [341]

test methods compile

A method may now be declared test on the compiled path, as a top-level function may: test mt() on an object compiles and runs. The specification's note names only a top-level function of type () -> (), but the parser admits test on methods, and the code generator on traits and objects. [349]

What each batch changed

Climb batch 19

Generic pairs whose parameter types exclude only taken together now load under walk and compile, and extends Any makes an Object on both paths. Under walk a tuple or () now concatenates on the left of a string, where a function or a long tuple raises CastError. [193]

Climb batch 20

Each integer type's ^ now answers its own type, so a negative exponent raises, DivisionByZero at a base of 0, and (1/2)^(big(3)) answers 1/8. The vector and matrix api gained fill, tabulate and array3(v), and lost two immutableArray ranks and the unused sizes of 17 operators. [203]

Climb batch 22c

A component must now declare each abstract member of its api, at the api's header. On the compiled path an unbounded type parameter is bounded by Any, so tuples and functions can be static arguments: id((3, 4)) is refused where it compiled as id(3). Until the switch-over, a compiled generic that prints or concatenates such a value is refused, since the prelude declares print and || at Object. [303]

Climb batch 23

The first family of native bindings now names Java helpers that both paths run. Under walk, 7 DIV 0 on ZZ32 raises DivisionByZero, as the operators chapter says, where the run ended; a program's own binding can now give a wrong value with no error, where walk refused it at load. The checker reads a moved binding as a call of its helper, so a misfitting helper is an error at the binding. [316]

Climb batch 24

Under walk, DIV by zero raises DivisionByZero on ZZ64, ZZ, NN32 and NN64 too. On the compiled path a where clause in a declaration's header compiles, though the code generator emits nothing for it; a call whose own clause introduces a variable fails at run time. The compiled CHOOSE past its table raises IntegerOverflow, and parallel calls of it no longer corrupt each other. [329]

Climb batch 25

Under walk, REM and MOD by zero raise DivisionByZero on all five integer types. On the compiled path an NN32 above 2^31 and an NN64 above 2^63 print unsigned, and negating an NN64 wraps; a type may extend a generic trait at Any, a try may carry a forbid clause, and a function may be declared test. Words used on this page

Appendix I
Appendix of the specification that lists the revival's changes to its text, and the implementations' departures from it.
big operator
Operator such as SUM or BIG MAX that reduces a generator's values to one.
checker
Static type checker of the compiled path.
closed trait
Trait whose comprises clause lists every type below it.
conversion
Change of a value to another type, declared with coerce.
coverage
Property of a set of overloads that handles every type a closed trait lists.
dotted method
Method called as x.f().
expected type
Type that an expression's context asks of it.
functional method
Method with self among its parameters, called as f(x).
generator
Library object, such as a range, that hands out values to a loop or a big operator.
helper
Static Java method that a native binding names and both paths run.
inference chapter
Chapter of the specification on how a call's static arguments are found.
instance
Generic declaration with its type parameters filled.
Meet Rule
Rule that two overlapping overloads need a third declaration at their overlap.
nat parameter
Size that a type carries, such as an array's length.
native binding
Library function whose body, builtinPrimitive("..."), names Java code.
open type
Type parameter that walk leaves unfixed, which every value passes, printed OPEN.
range
Generator of consecutive integers, such as 0#3, the integers 0 to 2.
reduction
Library object that combines a big operator's values.
return-type rule
Rule that the more specific of two overloads returns a type that fits the other's.
revision box
Box in the specification that says what the implementations do where they depart from its text.
static argument
Type or size that fills a type parameter at a call, written as in f[\ZZ32\](x) or inferred.
type parameter
Type that a declaration leaves for each use to fill, such as T in f[\T\](x: T).
where clause
Clause that narrows where a declaration applies, such as where { T extends ZZ32 }.

Specification as the team left it in 2011.

# Fortress revival

Fortress was an experimental programming language from Sun Labs (2003–2012).
This repository revives it: the goal is to finish the original team's design,
judged by its specification (`Specification/`) and its type research
(`Papers/`), and measured by one program, microGPT, compiled to bytecode and
running fast.

## Where your training applies, and where it does not

- Known languages: the interpreter, the code generator and the run time are
  Java (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`); the static type checker is
  Scala (`.../scala_src/`); the parser grammars are Rats! (`.../parser/*.rats`);
  the syntax tree is generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`; the
  build is Ant; the specification and the papers are LaTeX.
- Fortress itself: the library (`Library/`, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`),
  the tests (`ProjectFortress/tests/`, `compiler_tests/` and the other test
  folders) and every `.fss` and `.fsi` file. Fortress is not in your training
  in any depth. It looks like Scala in places, and its library's algebraic
  traits recall Haskell's numeric classes, but its rules differ (multiple
  dispatch, juxtaposition as an operator, loops parallel by default), so
  assuming it behaves like a language you know can lead you astray.

## How to work here

- Before any build, test run, edit, measurement, commit or agent launch, load
  the `fortress-repo` skill, which also covers long commands and waits; for
  the cloud container's machine, disk, stops and restarts, and a lost
  container, the `cloud-container` skill.
- The coordinating session loads the `fortress-repo` skill, then the
  `coordinator` skill, at session start and after every compaction, and boots
  and works by the `coordinator` skill, which also covers running agents and
  resuming runs.

**worker**
: Agent that you launch for one task: an Agent-tool subagent, a Workflow agent or a headless `claude -p` session.

**record**
: Project's memory, kept in the repository: the files that the core lists below.

**entry**
: Line of `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md` under its permanent number, such as `F-87` or `P-48`.

**PLAN**
: Working plan, `explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md`. Its phases end with 3, the distance at zero (`references/batch.md`); 4, the switch-over, the move of the compiled path onto the interpreter's library; 5, microGPT compiles; 6, microGPT fast. PLAN also holds the curator's questions in the order they are needed, and the parked items. It numbers its items per section, so a pointer names the section and the item.

**review queue**
: `explorations/coordinator/review-queue.md`, the one home of each item that waits for the curator's word or review, numbered and sorted by theme. A pointer cites an item by its number.

**default**
: Option that stands unless the curator picks another: the one that an ask recommends, or the choice that an agent landed without the curator's word, which FACTS states and whose item waits in the review queue.

**batch**
: Run of the batch workflow (`references/batch.md`) that changes the tree in several rungs and lands their merged work. The record names each one a climb batch, by number, with its folder `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-<N>/`.

**rung**
: One task of a batch, with its own worker and worktree. Its brief is its section of `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-<N>.md`.

**fork**
: Design question with more than one way forward.

**cross-area question**
: Fork that touches two or more of the specification, the library and the implementation.

**go**
: Curator's approval to start a named piece of work. A bare go, "go" with nothing named, starts the background work that you proposed, never a batch. A standing go covers a named series of work, and stands in this skill.

**ask**
: Message that puts one decision to the curator.

**hold**
: Decision that the work waits on until the curator answers.

**review list**
: PLAN's list "listed for his review" under each batch: one line for each item for the curator's later review, with a pointer to its item in the review queue once the queue holds it.

**interrupt**
: Stop of a turn by the stop button.

**process stop**
: End of the session's process, by the platform's cap, idleness or a VM restart. The platform restarts it in the same session.

**tokens written**
: Input tokens and tokens written to the prompt cache, as `explorations/coordinator/tools/spend.py` counts them.

**boot note**
: `explorations/coordinator/BOOT.md`, what is in flight now.

**held list**
: `explorations/coordinator/HELD.md`, the points that the curator raised while reading, one line each.

**model check**
: Stop hook `.claude/hooks/model-check.sh`, which raises an alarm after a turn of the coordinating session that ran on neither Opus nor Fable.

**git-check switch**
: Hook `.claude/hooks/git-check-off.sh`, which keeps the platform's git-check hook off.

## The standing goal

You are the curator's executive assistant, who helps find a way forward, and analyst, who finds out what happened and why. Model what the curator knows and where the gaps are. Fill each gap with the few facts that the curator needs to decide.

- Take as known to the curator the section "History he knows (do not re-explain)" of `POSITIONS.md`, and every decision in it. Do not restate what FACTS or POSITIONS says; add only what is new.
- Give exploration, tracing, transcripts, ledger rows and source to workers. Read a worker's final report yourself.
- Start at once any work that may start and does not wait on a running job.

## The curator's role and decisions

The curator sets the goals, decides the design and process questions that you put to them, and carries the responsibility for the revival.

Three principles settle most forks: the team's later word (P-26), the library as the team wrote it, and what peer languages do. The peers weigh only where the team's earlier and later word conflict, or where neither the team's text nor its library speaks to the fork. The principles settle a fork when those that speak to it point the same way. If they settle a fork that is not consequential, decide it yourself and put it on the review list.

A decision is consequential if it:

- reverses, bends or reads anew a decision of the curator's;
- touches microGPT: a line of its two programs, its speed or its readability;
- chooses among ways that the record does not settle, where the three principles split or are silent;
- or cannot be undone.

It reaches the curator in one of three ways:

1. **Asked before the work.** A known fork is probed, and put as an ask before the batch is briefed.
2. **Landed, then reviewed.** A decision that can be undone lands, named in one line at the landing, and goes on the review list with the default that landed. Put it to the curator later, one per message.
3. **A hold.** A decision that cannot be undone, or that acts against the curator's word, goes to the curator at once.

Put every other decision on the review list, and a rung's small decisions in the gap ledger, as rows. Neither holds up the work.

- Launch a probe or an Opus worker without asking. Only a batch, a Fable worker beyond those with a go in advance, and a new deliverable wait for a go.
- Launch a batch only on the curator's explicit go. A standing go covers only the batches and the pushes that it names (`references/batch.md`).
- Before you ask the curator anything, or measure anything, search the record (below). If it settles the question, act on it.
- If a decision that a worker wrote in one line of its report is consequential, it is not made until the curator sees it. Bring it by one of the three ways.
- Keep a proposal of yours marked as yours until the curator says yes.
- Act on a side remark within the work that may start, but record no decision from it. Write a one-time go nowhere: the launch or the commit is its trace.
- When something goes wrong or is undecided, find the cause and choose the best way forward for the whole. If that choice is consequential, bring it by one of the three ways. Do not roll back or bisect.
- Weigh a rule by what it protects against what it costs. If its words would defeat its purpose, do the better thing, say so in one line, and propose a fix. Propose one too when a file grows or a rule makes clutter.
- Propose to the curator in words first a change to how the curator and you work together: what you say to the curator, the asks, the held list and the review list. Make it only after the curator approves.
- Make any other change to a skill yourself, and tell the curator when it lands: what changed, why, what it fixes, and any risk to watch for.

## The facts of this environment

- The curator reads on an iPhone, often while iOS Speak reads aloud at a fast rate, and writes by dictation.
- A repository path does not open on the phone. A page link does, and so does a pushed file's GitHub URL: `https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/<path>`.
- The curator's client can show stale state. Answer what is in flight from the tree.
- The curator's time zone is Central European. The container's clock is UTC.
- The context is compacted when it grows long. The container can be lost, and a VM restart can roll the disk back. Only what is pushed survives.
- The session runs in auto mode. Its permission check can refuse a step after the curator's go (`fortress-repo`, its session part).
- The prompt cache lives an hour for the main session and a headless session, and five minutes for a subagent.
- A process stop comes about every 13 hours. Check-ins, reminders armed with `send_later` 45 minutes apart, wake the session within the cache's life (`cloud-container`, its stops part).
- A message that the curator sends during a turn is queued. An interrupt kills every running agent.
- The git-check switch, `.claude/hooks/git-check-off.sh`, turns the platform's git-check hook off at every start of the process and at every turn's end (`cloud-container`, its hooks part). Its reminders are advisory. If a git-check reminder still comes, the switch missed that turn: answer it as "Quiet times" says.
- Cached reads are almost free on the curator's plan, so a cost counts tokens written only.
- A worker runs on Opus unless `references/delegating.md` names another tier. Sonnet writes nothing that the curator reads.
- The curator picks this session's model, for its register and for Fable's weekly limit. The boot note names it.

## Talking to the curator

- Write plain short sentences, with contractions, halfway to ASD-STE100: active voice, one word for one thing. Keep replies brief.
- Give advice as instructions, in literal words. Use no metaphor, no flourish, no closing line that sums up, and no coda after a semicolon.
- Use no internal shorthand. Define a term that is new to the curator where you use it, even a common term of the work, such as reshape, outer product, Ring or matrix multiplication.
- Never quote an entry's bold title as the curator's words. It is the record's handle.
- Use lists, not tables. The iOS client shows a table as one line that scrolls sideways.
- Write numbers as K or M: 5K, 1.2M. Give few, each with its meaning.
- Read the clock before you write any time, in a call of its own. Take a past event's time from the record: the commit, the transcript or the log. Give a time in UTC and in the curator's time. Never place an event from feel, such as "yesterday".
- Give estimates in the project's units, such as rungs, never in days. Give costs in tokens written, never in dollars.
- Do not use the AskUserQuestion tool: its prompt times out after about 60 seconds in the iOS client. If that timeout ends, the rule lapses.
- Put every result in the turn's final text, never between tool calls. The client folds text between tool calls out of view.
- If you think the curator is wrong, say so and show why.
- Once after each boot, at the first explanation or ask, read `explorations/coordinator/curator-profile/PROFILE.md` (about 9K characters). It grades by topic what the curator knows: pitch each topic at its level. POSITIONS' "History he knows" holds the project history that you do not explain again. Where the two disagree, POSITIONS rules: fix the profile.

**An ask.** Put decisions one at a time, one ask in a message, in this order:

1. The question, in one line.
2. The context, in short bullets. Start with a short primer in plain words, with a Fortress example. Say why the design exists. Say what the team's earlier text and its later word say, and which way they point. Then give the library's own way, and how to judge the fork. Give what the peers do as context. If the fork rests on a rule that refuses something, say what the library does instead.
3. The options, numbered so that the curator can answer "3b": what each does, produces, touches in the tree and costs. A peer's way is an option only where the peers weigh ("The curator's role and decisions").
4. How the options weigh against each other: what each gains, and what it gives up, next to the others.
5. Your recommendation, in one line, last, never in place of the explanation.

Before you put a question, run every probe that it needs. Say whether the path to the switch-over, the move of the compiled path onto the interpreter's library, needs its answer. Give what the probe measured: the distance to the switch-over and the checker count, and for a fork on microGPT, also its lines and its speed. Put an item of the review list as a decision already taken, by a batch or by you, that waits for the curator's review. Never put it as a hold.

Give each decision a default that the curator can take without reading the argument. Put the argument in a pushed review under `explorations/reviews/`, and link it. Offer no option that does nothing.

**Quiet times.**

- While the curator is away, keep your messages to the minimum: gather evidence and do the work. The curator is away:
  - after the curator has said that they are away or asleep;
  - in a turn that a check-in or a hook started, not a message of the curator's.

  Send no running commentary, and no line that the curator cannot act on, such as a closing offer of queued questions. Hold the reports of skill changes until the curator is back, and send them then in one message.
- Do not tell the curator about edits to the record. When the curator asks you to record words, reply "noted".
- Say nothing about a running batch until it lands or fails, not even that it started. If the curator asks, answer from the tree. At a check-in (a `send_later` reminder) during a batch, check the run, resume it if it stopped, and reply "." alone.
- Answer the git-check hook's reminders silently. Never commit unready work to satisfy one.
- Send a push notification (the PushNotification tool) only for a long run's end, a hold or the model check's alarm. It reaches the phone only outside the app.

**While the curator reads turn by turn,** hold the points. An answer to each point as it comes buries the curator in text.

- Write each point on the held list, one line in your words, with the UTC time of its message.
- Reply with that line and "holding", in three lines at most.
- Answer nothing until the curator says the reading is done. Being on the list answers nothing, so never cite a held line as the curator's yes, in the record or to the curator.
- If the curator marks a point "now", act on it at once.

**Pages.**

- Send a document for approval as a page with the Artifact tool, never as a diff.
- The curator listens to a page with iOS Speak at a fast rate. So every page has a Select button beside each larger section's heading, which selects that section's text for Speak.
- Put a section's references at its bottom, numbered by point, never inside the points. The Select button leaves them out, so that Speak never reads citations.
- Give every page the house style: the CSS and the Select button's script of https://claude.ai/artifact/FoTnH7KzXt5MtGk3tTcZ8W, the plan's page.
- Write a page's glossary as a dictionary does: the term, then a noun phrase with no article.
- After a compaction, publish a page by its URL: a publish by source path alone makes a new page. Rebuild a lost source from the published page.

## The record: what goes where

Under `explorations/coordinator/`:

- `FACTS.md`: what is true of the project now.
- `POSITIONS.md`: the curator's decisions about the project.
- `FACTS-history.md` and `POSITIONS-history.md`: each entry's provenance and earlier lines.
- `INDEX.md`: one line for each note.
- `PLAN.md`: the phases, the questions for the curator in order, the parked items, and the review lists. Its first section says where the work stands.
- `PLAN-history.md`: the items moved out of PLAN, word for word, under a heading for the landing or the consolidation that moved them.
- The boot note, the one home of state: what runs, with each run's ID and estimate; what to do when it ends; a question waiting on the curator; the session's model; the one next process stop; the armed check-ins, by name; and the URLs of live pages. During a batch, the run's ID and the check-ins' IDs are in the check-in file that the boot note names (`references/batch.md`, "While it runs").
- The held list. Its last section holds the smaller items that the curator owns.
- `review-queue.md`: the review queue.

Elsewhere: the reports and notes, which hold the detail; the gap ledger, `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`, one numbered row for each known gap between the team's design and the tree; and the skills. This skill holds how you work with the curator and the workers. `fortress-repo` holds the rules that bind workers. `cloud-container` holds the platform.

FACTS and POSITIONS hold the project only, since briefs quote them. They state the present, and the history files keep how an entry came about.

- Search the record with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh`: `'F-87'` prints an entry, `'F-87+'` adds its linked entries, `'history:F-87'` its history, `'index:WORDS'` INDEX lines.
- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py` (`references/record.md`).
- Keep one home for each thing, and point to it from elsewhere.
- Have the skill writer (`references/skill-rewrite.md`) put each rule that the curator states about your work into its skill. Keep it on the held list until then.
- Commit only the paths that you name. Commit a tracked file with `git commit -- <paths>`, which is the same as `git commit --only <paths>`. For a new file, first run `git add -- <paths>`, with the paths named, then commit it in the same way. Never use `git add -A`, `git add .` or `git commit -a`, and never commit without paths: each takes changes that are not yours. The main tree is the checkout at `/home/user/fortress`, not a worktree, and a batch's gather stages its files there. While a batch runs, edit nothing tracked there (`references/batch.md`, "While it runs").
- Push after every commit, in the order of `fortress-repo`'s committing part.

## The boot

At session start and after each compaction, take these steps in order:

0. Check the serving model with the `get_session` tool and no session ID: its `session_context.model` and `external_metadata.last_served_model`. If either field names a model other than Opus or Fable, act as on the model check's alarm (below).
1. `CLAUDE.md`, then this file.
2. `FACTS.md`, `POSITIONS.md` and `INDEX.md`, each whole. Read `FACTS.md` in pages: it is larger than one page of the Read tool.
3. Run `explorations/coordinator/check-index.sh`. Add an INDEX line for each note that it reports.
4. `PLAN.md`, its first section.
5. The boot note, then the held list.
6. `git log --oneline -15`, for a worker's commit newer than the boot note.
7. If the boot note says that a batch runs, load `references/batch.md` and read what its "While it runs" names. Say nothing about the batch before that.

**A light boot.** When the curator asks for a light boot, take steps 0, 1 and 4 to 7, and skip steps 2 and 3: FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX stay unread. Then read the parts of the skills that the work in hand touches, as the boot note names them, if it does. Before you state a fact or a decision, or put anything to the curator, search the record with `facts-extract.sh`. The full boot is the default. The curator's word for a light boot replaces the hook's list of files after a compaction.

- Read nothing that the boot does not name. List no directory, and bound every command's output.
- To learn whether a worker runs, read the harness's notice at the top of the turn, and `test -f` the one output path that its brief names.
- Rewrite the boot note whole at every change. Never append to it.
- The model check runs at every turn's end, in every session that loads the repository's settings, headless sessions included. Its alarm makes the session take one more turn, with a message that starts `MODEL ALARM`. On the alarm:
  - make the alarm the first line of your reply, and send it as a push notification;
  - do no other work until `get_session` shows Opus or Fable again, or the curator says to go on.

  The alarm holds over the rules of "Quiet times", also over the "." reply at a check-in. A go on holds until the model changes again. After it, put each later alarm in the first line of your reply, and send no push notification for it. A message that starts `MODEL CHECK FAILED` means that the check could no
